title: Writing the Rehat Maryada
hook: from the 1930s scholars and leaders drafted a shared code, published in 1950

segments.voice: Yesterday, Master Tara Singh, and your line was the teacher-leader. Did you thank someone who taught you? Today, a different kind of work: not a march, but a document. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

Who does the dishes? When do the lights go out? Do phones come to the table? Writing down a family's house rules sounds simple until everyone has an opinion, and every opinion comes with a story about how Grandma did it. Now make the family a whole panth, spread across villages and cities and countries, with customs that grew up differently in different places. And try to write one short booklet that they can share. That's today.
screen: `WRITING DOWN THE HOUSE RULES.` → `EVERYONE HAS AN OPINION.` → `ONE BOOKLET FOR A WHOLE PANTH.`

segments.voice: First, the need. Once the gurdwaras were in the sangat's hands, a practical question followed: how should things be done inside them, and in a Sikh's own life? Practices varied from place to place. The reformers wanted a shared standard. Second, the drafting. Under the SGPC, scholars, granthis and leaders met over years, wrote drafts, sent them out for comment, argued and revised. It was slow work. A code that only a few people wrote would be a code only a few people kept. Third, the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada opens by saying who a Sikh is: one who believes in the One Immortal Being, in the ten Gurus from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' teaching, and in the amrit given by the tenth Guru, and who holds to no other religion. Then it covers the daily prayers, how to sit before the Guru Granth Sahib, the ardas, the langar, the birth of a child, marriage and death, and the amrit ceremony. That's today's line: a code, agreed. Fourth, what agreed means. It doesn't mean every Sikh group signed every line. Some, like the Akhand Kirtani Jatha we'll meet tomorrow, the Damdami Taksal and Nihang groups, keep their own rehat on certain points. The SGPC's code guides the gurdwaras it manages, and others beyond them, and it sits alongside those others. What it gave the panth was a shared starting page: a place to point to and say, this is how we do it here.
screen: `HOW SHOULD THINGS BE DONE?` · `YEARS OF DRAFTS AND DEBATE.` · `WHO IS A SIKH, AND HOW TO LIVE.` · `A SHARED STARTING PAGE.` · then, large: `A CODE, AGREED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes toward your own short code. Sit, and let your breath slow. Ask yourself a simple question: what are three things I want to do, every day, no matter what? Not big promises. Small things: wake and sit quietly, speak honestly, share something. Let one come to mind, and hold it for a few breaths. Then a second. Then a third. Don't write yet; just notice which ones stay. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Writing the Rehat Maryada. The years of drafting and debate under the SGPC that produced a shared code of Sikh life and practice. Rehat is the way of living; maryada, the accepted custom. Today's word.
Your line: a code, agreed. Today, write your own simple code: three short lines on a card or in your phone, and read them once before bed. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras managed by the SGPC, and Sikh families who choose it, follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada published by the SGPC for daily prayers, services, the ardas and ceremonies; some Sikh groups keep their own rehat on certain points.

notes: Editor: rewrote the hook's opening, which told the listener what they know, as a run of questions; changed 'slow on purpose' to 'slow work' (and in the fork reveal) because the drafters' intent isn't stated in the cited sources.
The index hook names the 1930s and 1950; under the claims rule the voice gives no years and says 'over years'. A Keeper may wish to restore the dates if the SGPC edition's own preface states them.
Definition of a Sikh paraphrased from Article I; please check the paraphrase carefully.

The list of groups keeping their own rehat (Akhand Kirtani Jatha, Damdami Taksal, Nihang groups) and the phrase 'guides the gurdwaras it manages, and others beyond them' should be checked for fairness and accuracy.
Glosses: rehat as 'the way of living', maryada as 'the accepted custom'; please confirm.
McLeod is cited for the drafting history; a Keeper may prefer a Sikh-authored source.
Audit: pronunciation syllables corrected to mar-YAA-daa.
